storm.summary_layperson: Scattered thunderstorm cells are moving through the region from the north and northwest this evening, with a couple tracked toward the cove in the next hour or so — but without the Sound's usual cooling cushion in play tonight, the cove won't get any special protection from them.
storm.local_effect_blurb: Sound water (74°F) and air (73°F) are almost the same temperature tonight, so there's no stabilizing marine layer to weaken these storms before they reach the cove.
storm.detail_html:
Radar shows a cluster of showers and thunderstorms scattered across the wider metro area, consistent with the NWS forecast discussion's note of "weak forcing and weak low-level instability" supporting a slight chance of storms. Multiple cells in the 38–47 dBZ range sit within 6–16 miles of the cove, mostly to the north, northwest, and northeast.

Normally the cool Sound builds a stabilizing marine layer that weakens storms crossing the water. Not tonight: water and air temperature are within 0.5°F of each other, so the marine-layer protective mechanism is inactive. Shear is a moderate 18 kt and CAPE is modest at 610–750 J/kg — not enough instability for major intensification, and there are no active NWS watches or warnings.

Timing is layered: a fast-moving cell 14 miles NNE, closing at 22 kt, is projected to graze the area first, around 4:53 PM — just before this window opens. The pipeline's primary tracked cell, 12.7 miles NNW and closing slowly at 9 kt, is expected around 5:35 PM (window 5:16–5:55 PM, radar-measured motion, medium confidence). A third cell 15 miles N, closing at 12.5 kt, could add a second wave near 5:21 PM.

Most likely outcome: the cove sees a couple of quick shower or thunderstorm passes clustered in the 4:50–6:00 PM stretch, with a risk similar to surrounding inland towns since there's no Sound-effect cushion tonight. No additional cells are currently classified as closing beyond that window, so the risk should ease through the rest of the evening.

What would change the call: any of the 40+ dBZ cells reclassifying to a shorter-ETA "closing" status, CAPE building past 1,500 J/kg (HRRR shows it trending up from 610 toward ~1,040 J/kg over the next few hours), or an NWS watch/warning being issued would push this toward high risk.

arrival.blurb: Radar-tracked cell 12.7 mi NNW closing slowly at 9 kt; with no marine layer active tonight, don't expect the Sound to weaken or delay it — treat the window as a real ETA, not a cushioned one.

wind.tactics_blurb: A light, no-sea-breeze evening further complicated by thunderstorm cells passing north and northeast of the cove — expect gusty, shifting wind early in the window that settles into light and variable gradient flow later. Stay flexible near the middle of the course and treat any puff as short-lived.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Tonight is a gradient-only, no-sea-breeze day: the inland-vs-Sound temperature differential is essentially flat (−0.5°F), and only 10% of coastal stations are showing the southerly flow that would signal a thermal sea breeze. With the thermal driver absent, this is regime B regardless of magnitude, and the light gradient wind (ensemble authoritative mean 5 kt) puts it in the light-gradient bucket.

The wind field is unusually fragmented right now — direction agreement across the 29-station ensemble is just 0.24, far below the 0.6–0.8 range that would call a coherent field. That's consistent with several thunderstorm cells and their outflow boundaries crossing the area at different bearings rather than a single clean flow. With no consistent geographic edge to lean on, favor the center of the course rather than committing to either shore.

Shift character is erratic, not tactical — this isn't the clean oscillation of a mature sea breeze or the one-way rotation of a frontal passage; it's outflow-driven gusting that can reverse direction in minutes as cells pass. Expect the roughest, gustiest stretch (RYC already gusting to 9 kt against a 2–5 kt sustained base) in the first hour or two of the window while cells are actively closing, easing to a more settled light-and-variable gradient by 19:00–20:00.

Worth flagging: HRRR's raw forecast direction (ESE, ~108° for the top of the window) diverges sharply from the current RYC observation (SSE, 151°) — a 138° gap. That's well past the threshold where the two should be trusted equally; direction confidence for this window is low, and the hourly directions below should be read as a rough envelope, not a precise forecast, especially while storms are nearby.

For racers: this points to drifter-class conditions (2–7 kt sustained) punctuated by brief mid-teens gusts near passing cells, then trailing off to light and shifty by full dark. Not a night to count on pressure holding anywhere specific — play what you see boat-to-boat.
